tier_reason: First-party README numbers (672 vs 813 ms encode, 266 vs 344 ms decode, 31/31, z = 5.57) with no CPU model, compiler or flags, and the FLAC timing harness, its command lines and the timed 180 s clip are not published (remade_ffmpeg_rs tools/flac_gate.ps1 only covers interop and size; corpus/ is not in the repo). Tier stays C; the downgrade is for the overstated smaller-file claim.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Single-core, pinned, CPU time on one 180 s 44.1 kHz stereo music clip against FFmpeg 8.1.2's native flac: encode at -compression_level 8 672 ms vs 813 ms (0.83x, 17.3% faster), decode of an FFmpeg-encoded stream 266 ms vs 344 ms (0.77x, 22.7% faster), 31/31 paired wins on both (z = 5.57 is the sign-test value for 31/31). Smaller-file claim (20 of 20 gate combos, e.g. stereo guitar s24 L8 539,087 vs 565,122 bytes) is inflated: FFmpeg's flac muxer writes an 8,192-byte PADDING block by default (libavformat/flacenc.c, metadata_header_padding = -1 becomes 8192) plus a Vorbis comment, which flac_gate.ps1 does not disable, while rusty_flac writes only fLaC + STREAMINFO. Subtracting roughly 8.2 KB of metadata (derived from page data): guitar s24 about -3.2% and piano s16 about -1.1% remain, but pink noise s24 (delta 8,100 B), vocal s16 (8,024 B) and silence (7,964 B) become ties or slightly larger for rusty_flac.
corrections.workload: Single-core comparison, both binaries pinned to one core at High priority, ABBA-alternated, 31 pairs, on a 180 s 44.1 kHz stereo music clip (guitar, piano, vocal): encode at -compression_level 8, and decode of an FFmpeg-encoded stream. Per the README, outputs are verified lossless before timing; the public tools/flac_gate.ps1 checks lossless round trips in both directions (SHA-256 of decoded PCM) and sizes on 10 clips x levels 5 and 8, but the timing harness itself is not published.
corrections.hardware: CPU model not stated ('single core, this machine'). The gate script's default FFmpeg path is a Windows Gyan 'ffmpeg-8.1.2-full_build' package, so the box is a Windows x86-64 PC (inferred); four AVX2 kernels are runtime-detected.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the timed builds. Cargo.toml only sets edition 2021 and rust-version 1.85 (minimum); no RUSTFLAGS or target-cpu are given. FFmpeg arm is the prebuilt Gyan 'ffmpeg-8.1.2-full_build' Windows binary (default path in remade_ffmpeg_rs tools/flac_gate.ps1).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1 star, 0 forks; crates.io rusty_flac 1,348 total downloads (0.1.0 on 2026-08-13 to 0.2.0 on 2026-09-30); README claims 321 active installs via one downstream app (RAG Converter), not verifiable
corrections.caveats: Rust crate, not C++ (wave language filter mismatch). First-party claim: CPU model, compiler and rustc flags are not stated, and the pinned ABBA CPU-time harness for FLAC is not identifiable in remade_ffmpeg_rs tools/bench (pinab.py reads a self-reported time with a kbps argument; codec-bench.ps1 is a video-frame harness), so its command lines (for example whether FFmpeg got -threads 1) are unknown. Like-for-like on threading: both arms are pinned to one core and FFmpeg's flac encoder is single-threaded; FFmpeg's flac decoder has frame threading (AV_CODEC_CAP_FRAME_THREADS), so without -threads 1 any extra FFmpeg threads would share the pinned core and add overhead to the FFmpeg decode arm. All four timing figures are integer multiples of the Windows 15.625 ms CPU-time tick (43, 52, 17 and 22 ticks, derived from page data), the clock the group's own codec-bench.ps1 calls tick accounting rather than a clock; the gaps are 9 and 5 ticks, so the direction is plausible but each ratio has about 2-6% resolution. Single 180 s clip for speed; the timed clip and the corpus are not published. Compression levels do not do the same work: rusty_flac's level maps to LPC order only with estimate-gated search, FFmpeg's level 8 uses its own order-search method. The smaller-file claim is inflated by FFmpeg's default 8,192-byte PADDING block (see claimed_speedup); on pink noise, vocal and silence rusty_flac's audio payload is not smaller. The baseline is FFmpeg's flac, not the reference libFLAC, which was not tested. Lossless interop is gated in public code (flac_gate.ps1) on 20 clip-level combos. Young project with rapid release churn (48 commits, v0.2.0 on 2026-09-30).

notes: Speed numbers are on the README and plausible but first-party and tick-quantized; the 20/20 smaller-file headline largely reflects FFmpeg's default 8 KiB metadata padding, verified in FFmpeg 8.1 libavformat/flacenc.c and rusty_flac src/encode.rs. Language is Rust, outside the C++ filter. Unlike other Remade-With-Rust repos, this one compares single core against single core.

tier_reason: The author's own PDF (doc/SuperFast Codecs.pdf) gives the '3x with four threads' sentence and two bar charts (FAAC and Opus, 1T/4T/8T, regular vs SuperFast) with no units, CPU model, OS, compiler or codec versions; no benchmark script is in the repo. First-party with no methodology, so C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Text: 'Using four threads, the conversion is already three times faster than with the regular drivers, which use only a single thread in this mode' (single file mode); in multi file mode the SuperFast drivers are 'only slightly faster'. Chart readings (approximate, unit-less y axis, derived from page data): single file mode, regular drivers about 24 (FAAC) and 29 (Opus) at every thread setting; SuperFast about 8.2 / 9.0 at 4 threads (about 2.9x / 3.2x) and 5.3 / 6.1 at 8 threads (about 4.5x / 4.8x); SuperFast at 1 thread is about 4% faster from decode/encode thread separation. Multi file mode gains are about 1-10%. Only FAAC and Opus are charted; Core Audio, FDK-AAC, LAME and Speex have no published numbers.
corrections.workload: Converting one input file to one output file (single file mode) or several files in parallel (multi file mode) in fre:ac with 1, 4 or 8 threads, FAAC and Opus only. Each worker runs its own codec instance on overlapping blocks: the 2017 PDF describes 128-frame blocks with 8-frame overlap, while the archived repo's Opus driver uses 256-frame blocks with an overlap of at least 24 frames, and the LAME driver uses 128-frame blocks with 4x1152/frameSize overlap plus a frame repacker. Default thread count is cores + (logical CPUs - cores)/2.
corrections.caveats: First-party PDF whose numbers are only in chart images with no y-axis unit; CPU model, OS, compiler and codec versions are not stated (the text only says 'even on a 6 core CPU'), and no benchmark script is published, so tier C. The measured code does different work from the baseline: it is the same codec run as several parallel instances against one single-threaded instance, not a faster codec implementation, and total CPU work rises because overlap frames are encoded and then discarded (6.25% at 8/128 in the PDF, about 9.4% at 24/256 in the final Opus driver). Output is not bit-identical to a single-threaded encode: every chunk starts from fresh encoder state, and the PDF's difference-signal plots show residual differences the author calls 'unnoticeable' without any listening test, objective quality metric or bitrate/size comparison. For MP3 the LAME driver unpacks and repacks frames to rebuild the bit reservoir across chunk seams, with rate-control limits and re-encoding when a frame does not fit. In multi file mode the gain is small (about 1-10%). The Opus resampler stays single-threaded, so non-48 kHz input gains less, and conversions are often limited by decoding speed. Repo archived 2020-12-11 (last commit 2020-12-10, last code change 2018-09-01); the code lives on in enzo1982/BoCA.

notes: Quote and both modes check out against the PDF; the chart image shows only FAAC and Opus at 1T/4T/8T, so I added approximate chart readings and the overlap/quality trade-off from components/opus/opus.cpp and components/lame/lame.cpp. No machine is named.

tier_reason: BENCHMARKS.md (2023-02-03) is first-party. The harness is public (hyperfine command, symphonia-play --decode-only, pdeljanov/FFmpeg symphonia-ffbench doc/examples/ffbench.c), CPUs are named and rustc 1.67.0 with -C target-cpu=native is given, but the FFmpeg compiler, version and flags are not stated and the test files are the author's unpublished media, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Relative decode time Symphonia/FFmpeg (below 1.0 means Symphonia is faster). i7-4790K: FLAC 0.71-0.74, ALAC 0.73-0.79, MP1 0.45-0.48, MP2 0.60, MP3 320 kbps 0.84, ADPCM IMA 0.83. M1 Pro: FLAC 0.51-0.64, ALAC 0.77-0.81, MP1 0.63-0.64, MP2 0.72-0.77, ADPCM MS 0.59, MP3 320 kbps 0.81. Raspberry Pi 4B: FLAC 0.96-1.04, ALAC 0.81-0.88, MP1 0.83-0.87, MP2 0.91-0.93, MP3 320 kbps 0.95, ADPCM MS 0.96. Slower than FFmpeg on AAC-LC (1.10-1.27), Vorbis (1.05-1.24) and MP3 128 kbps (1.00-1.07) everywhere, and on ADPCM MS on the i7-4790K (1.13) and ADPCM IMA on the M1 Pro (1.51) and Pi (1.05). The README summarises this as 'generally +/-15%' of FFmpeg.
corrections.caveats: Rust library, not C++ (wave language filter mismatch). First-party results, so tier C: the test files come from the author's personal media library (not published) and only one or two files are used per codec, which the page itself says favours the decoders it was tuned on. The page was last updated 2023-02-03 (rustc 1.67.0, development main of both projects at that date), long before the current v0.6.1, so the numbers may be stale. The FFmpeg C compiler, version and flags are not stated (plain ./configure). Timings are whole-process hyperfine wall times (startup and demuxing included for both; ffbench is statically linked). Results are mixed: Symphonia loses on AAC-LC, Vorbis and MP3 128 kbps everywhere and on ADPCM on some CPUs, and wins mainly on FLAC, ALAC, MP1 and MP2; on the Raspberry Pi the margins are small (10 of 16 rows faster, 0.81-0.96). Like-for-like single thread: ffbench.c opens the decoder with avcodec_open2(dec_ctx, dec, NULL), so libavcodec's default of one thread applies even for FLAC and ALAC, which support frame threading.

notes: All quoted ratios match BENCHMARKS.md; I added the omitted ADPCM losses (i7 ADPCM MS 1.13, M1 ADPCM IMA 1.51, Pi ADPCM IMA 1.05) and fixed the claim that it loses on most Pi codecs (it wins 10 of 16 rows there). FFmpeg single-threaded confirmed from ffbench.c. Language is Rust, outside the C++ filter.
